--- title: "Why optimal-excitation system ID" description: "An evidence-based comparison of optimal-excitation frequency-domain identification (Pintelon–Schoukens) against broadband random noise and swept sine — with head-to-head campaigns from the system_ident package, and an account of when each alternative is the appropriate choice." freeze: true --- This page sets out the measurement method `system_ident` implements — an optimal-excitation, periodic-multisine, frequency-domain identification in the [Pintelon–Schoukens](overview.qmd) ("P&S") tradition — and weighs it against the two excitations most subsystems reach for first: broadband random noise and the swept sine. It is written for engineers in any LIGO subsystem — suspensions, seismic/ISI, DARM/calibration, ALS, OMC — because the argument concerns the measurement, not the plant. The claim is not that the multisine is always preferable. It is narrower: when measurement time is expensive, drive is bounded, the plant is high-Q, and the loop is closed, optimal-excitation ID delivers more parameter precision per second and per count of drive than the alternatives, and the margin is measured here rather than asserted. Where a swept sine or random noise is the appropriate tool, this page says so. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Everything below is a real package run Every number and figure comes from the glue module `docs/method_demo.py`, which runs the campaigns through the library internals (`SysIDLoop._estimate_tf_periodic`, `optimal_excitation`, `fisher.parameter_covariance`, `run_siso_passes`). The page is rendered with `freeze: true`. No number on this page is hand-entered; if a result is mixed, the text says so. ::: ::: {#20c636c4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue (runs the real campaigns)"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "method_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "method_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np from IPython.display import display import method_demo as md ``` ::: ## 1 · The measurement problem, and the figures of merit Every subsystem identification has the same shape: a plant with sharp, high-Q resonances packed into a narrow band, observed through a noisy readout, driven by an actuator with a hard amplitude limit, often inside a closed loop, and allotted only so much observing time before the instrument must go back to work. ::: {#afa76528 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="A representative suspension plant over its readout floor"} md.problem_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: A method is therefore good or bad only relative to what it costs and returns. Every excitation here is scored on the same five figures of merit: - **Parameter / FRF uncertainty per unit time** — the Cramér–Rao σ (or σ/θ) reached for a given total measurement time. - **Uncertainty per unit in-band drive power** — the same σ for a given RMS (in-band power) budget. Drive is ultimately capped by actuator saturation, so this is a hard currency too. RMS is reported plant-referred; the peak that binds is set at the DAC, after the whitening/actuation chain this simulation does not model (see §2.1 and §9). - **Leakage bias** — whether the estimator reads a sharp resonance at its true height or smears it. This is a bias no amount of averaging removes. - **Per-bin noise model** — whether the method measures its own error bar at each frequency or requires one to be assumed. - **Safety** — whether the method is safe to run closed-loop, and how much in-band drive power it asks of the actuator. The rest of this page is those five columns, filled with measured numbers. ## 2 · The three excitations All three put energy into the plant and observe the response. They differ in how that energy is distributed in frequency and time, and that difference accounts for the rest. ::: {#622ed6fb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="The same in-band power as swept sine, random noise, and a multisine"} md.excitations_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - **Swept sine** drives one frequency at a time, dwelling long enough to beat down noise at that line. It is leakage-free per line, directly interpretable, and spends all its power where it is pointed, but it visits the band serially. - **Broadband random noise** drives every frequency at once with random phase. It is the fastest route to a qualitative whole-band picture and a coherence estimate, but it is not periodic, so its DFT leaks, and a single record gives no internal error bar. - **Periodic multisine** also drives every frequency at once, with a period exactly equal to the analysis window, tiled and repeated. That periodicity — not the choice of phase — is what makes the measurement leakage-free and self-error-barred, and it is the substrate the optimal design shapes. The line phases are a free choice (the package defaults to Schroeder); as §2.1 shows, they do not affect the FRF or its error bar. The crest factors printed above are measured but plant-referred — peak/RMS of the digital request, not of the waveform at the actuator's hard limit. Because crest factor is not invariant under filtering, a low plant-referred crest does not imply a low crest at the DAC once a whitening/actuation chain sits in between. This page therefore claims no crest- or peak-drive advantage from phasing; §2.1 sets out that argument in full. ### 2.1 · Phasing: Schroeder vs random, a plant-referred fact A multisine's line phases are free: they set only the time-domain crest factor (peak/RMS) of the drive. It is worth being precise about what that does and does not achieve, because the textbook framing — "Schroeder phases minimise the crest factor, so a saturation-limited actuator carries more power" — holds only in a reference frame this simulation cannot reach. **Schroeder is lower-crest in plant-referred units.** The package default (`phase="schroeder"`) minimises peak/RMS of the requested waveform; random phasing does not. The gap is real and grows with the number of lines: ::: {#d7cd9a2e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Real crest factors: Schroeder vs random, vs number of lines (flat broadband)"} ph = md.phasing_crest_campaign() md.phasing_crest_fig(ph) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Schroeder sits near a constant ≈1.9 regardless of line count; random phasing climbs as ≈√(ln N), from comparable at a handful of lines to roughly 2× worse across hundreds of flat lines. On the concentrated optimal ASD this page actually drives with — a couple dozen significant lines piled at the modes — the gap is much smaller: ::: {#4b70a4a8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Crest on the concentrated optimal ASD vs a flat one (printed inline)"} display(md.phasing_shape_md(ph)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} - **flat spectrum** (628 bins): Schroeder crest **1.84**, random **3.63 ± 0.31** — random is 1.97× higher. - **concentrated optimal ASD** (~26 significant lines): Schroeder crest **1.93**, random **2.65 ± 0.27** — random only 1.37× higher. ::: ::: So in plant-referred units Schroeder is lower-crest, but for the few concentrated lines the optimal design uses, the margin over random is modest (~1.4×) rather than the order of magnitude the "hard actuator limit" framing implies. **Phasing does not change the measurement.** The leakage-free FRF and its Cramér–Rao bound depend on the line amplitudes and power, not the phases — the CRB function does not take phase as an argument. Driving the same plant with the same PSD and the same noise seeds, Schroeder and random phasing recover statistically identical FRFs, identical per-bin σ, and an identical CRB: ::: {#2c46dfe7 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Phase-invariance of the estimate: Schroeder vs random, same plant/PSD/seeds"} pin = md.phasing_invariance_campaign() display(md.phasing_invariance_table(pin)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **The estimate is phase-invariant: over 8 seeds the recovered FRF, its per-bin σ, and the CRB are identical within scatter — the CRB does not even take phase as an input (it is a function of the line PSD). Phase changes only the plant-referred crest factor, which this sim cannot refer to the DAC.** | figure of merit (same plant, same PSD, same seeds) | Schroeder phase | random phase | | --- | --- | --- | | RMS frac. FRF error to truth (coh>0.9) | 14.37% ± 0.32% | 14.49% ± 0.33% | | median per-bin σ(FRF) | 0.000353 | 0.000353 | | Cramér–Rao worst-parameter σ | 14.5 | 14.5 | ::: ::: **Why the crest margin does not transfer — the DAC reference frame.** In LIGO the actuator's hard saturation limit lives at the DAC (counts/volts), and there are whitening and actuation filters between the digital excitation request and the DAC. Crest factor is not invariant under filtering: the whitening filter reshapes the waveform and scrambles the optimised Schroeder phases, so the DAC-frame crest is generally higher and unrelated to the plant-referred crest minimised above. Minimising crest in plant units therefore has no effect at the DAC — the limit that binds — and this simulation does not model the whitening chain, so it cannot represent the DAC frame at all. ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} ## Phasing: the conclusion Phase touches only the crest factor, and crest is a DAC-frame quantity this plant-referred simulation does not model. Since the estimate is phase-invariant (table above) and the one quantity phase affects does not transfer to the binding limit, the phase choice is not load-bearing here: random phases are as good as Schroeder for these purposes. A crest or peak-drive optimisation is a DAC-frame, filter-aware problem — pushing the optimisation through the whitening chain — and is future work rather than a claim this page makes from plant-referred numbers. ::: ## 3 · Broadband random noise leaks, and is variance-inefficient The case against random noise is not aesthetic. On a high-Q resonance — where the information lives — a windowed transform of a one-off random record biases the peak low, because the sharp mode leaks its power into neighbouring bins. The leakage-free multisine, given the same plant, the same power, and the same wall-clock, does not. ::: {#c207ac40 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Same high-Q mode, same power, same time: leakage-free vs windowed random"} c_leak = md.leakage_campaign(seed=0) md.leakage_bode_fig(c_leak) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The multisine markers sit on the true peak with tight error bars; the windowed-Welch points read the resonance low. Repeating both over several noise realisations separates the two failure modes, bias (leakage) and scatter (variance): ::: {#411b8d33 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Peak-bin bias and scatter over several seeds"} v_leak = md.leakage_variance(n_seeds=8) display(md.leakage_table(v_leak)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **High-Q peak recovery (Q=60, linewidth ≈2.1 bins): the random estimator is biased AND noisier — combined it is 31× worse at the peak** | peak-bin figure of merit | leakage-free multisine | windowed random (Welch) | truth | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | peak-bin estimate (mean) | 453.5 | 381.1 | 455.9 | | bias vs truth | -0.5% | -16.4% | 0 | | scatter (std, 8 seeds) | 0.00 | 20.30 | — | | peak RMSE (bias+scatter) | 2.47 | 77.54 | — | ::: ::: The random estimator is biased and noisier; combined as RMSE at the peak it is many times worse than the leakage-free multisine carrying identical power for identical time. This is the principal reason the package never identifies with random noise: the bias is systematic, it lands on the high-Q features the measurement exists to characterise, and averaging longer does not remove it. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## When random noise is the right tool For a qualitative whole-band look, a quick coherence check, or any broadband floor or disturbance characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant, colored random noise is fast, simple, and appropriate — and `excitation.timeseries_from_asd` exists for that. The argument here is against using it as the quantitative FRF estimator on a sharp resonance. ::: ## 4 · The serial coverage cost of the swept sine The swept sine has no leakage problem and no crest-factor problem — it spends full power on one clean line at a time. Its cost is time: it tours the band serially. The multisine measures every bin in one window; in that same wall-clock the sweep reaches only a handful of frequencies, each of them tight, because it spends full power there. ::: {#bd95b49f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="σ(FRF)/|FRF| — whole-band multisine vs equal-wall-clock swept sine"} c_sweep = md.sweep_campaign(seed=0) md.sweep_fig(c_sweep) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The sweep points sit on or below the multisine envelope — full power per line gives low σ at each visited frequency — but there are only a few of them. Covering the whole band to the same per-bin σ costs the sweep the factor annotated on the plot, here roughly two orders of magnitude longer than the one multisine window. On a real instrument that is the difference between a measurement that fits inside a maintenance window and one that does not. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## When the swept sine is the right tool For a single line — one calibration tone, one resonance to be pinned to high SNR, a quick spot check — the swept sine is the obvious choice, since all the available power goes to the one frequency of interest. It is also the most transparent to interpret. The multisine applies when the whole band is needed. ::: ## 5 · Time and in-band drive under the optimal design So far the multisine has matched the alternatives where they are weak. The principal result is the allocation: spend the drive budget not flat across the band, but concentrated where the Fisher information is. `design.pintelon.optimal_excitation` solves for that allocation by the dispersion-function fixed point (see [Fisher & excitation](fisher.qmd)). ::: {#608208ab .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="The optimal drive concentrates power at the modes; CRB variance-reduction F"} head = md.headline_campaign() md.headline_design_fig(head) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The gold drive concentrates power onto the two resonances instead of spreading it flat. The Cramér–Rao variance-reduction factor `F` — worst-parameter, at equal power and time, from `fisher.parameter_covariance` — is annotated on the design panel. That factor is the budget the optimal design has to spend, and it can be taken in either of two forms: ::: {#b5cc0fee .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Three real campaigns: flat, optimal (same power), optimal (matched σ)"} md.headline_convergence_fig(head) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#9cccc3cc .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Side by side: σ reached, and the drive it took"} display(md.headline_table(head)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Same plant, same 4 passes. At equal power the optimal drive reaches 5.0× lower σ in fewer passes (the time win); dialled to P/F it MATCHES flat's σ at 3.8× less in-band drive power (RMS, F=14 from the CRB). RMS is plant-referred; the binding actuator limit is DAC saturation after the whitening/actuation chain, which this sim does not model — so no peak/crest advantage is claimed.** | excitation | drive power | RMS drive (plant-referred) | final σ/θ | passes to σ/θ≤0.05 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | flat multisine | P | 1.00 | 0.074 | — | | optimal multisine | P | 1.00 | 0.015 | 2 | | optimal multisine | P/14 | 0.27 | 0.055 | — | ::: ::: Both rows of the optimal arm matter: - **At equal drive power**, the optimal multisine reaches a parameter uncertainty several times lower than the flat drive in the same number of passes; the flat drive does not cross the σ/θ target inside the budget, while the optimal drive crosses it in a couple of passes. This is the time reduction, and it is frame-robust: a statement about Fisher information per second, independent of any actuator unit. - **Reduced to power P/F**, the optimal multisine instead matches the flat drive's σ, at a fraction of the in-band drive power (RMS). This is the drive reduction: the same result for materially less in-band power asked of the actuator. The RMS figures are plant-referred. No peak- or crest-drive claim is made: concentrating power does raise the plant-referred crest, but as §2.1 showed, plant-referred crest does not transfer to the DAC — the limit that binds — through the unmodelled whitening chain. The load-bearing results here are the time (whole-band simultaneity) and the CRB allocation of in-band power, both frame-robust. The two cannot be had simultaneously — `F` is a single budget — but which scarce resource (time or in-band drive power) it is spent on is a choice. Flat excitation offers neither. ## 6 · Identification inside a closed loop {#a-closed-loop-is-not-an-obstacle} Most LIGO plants are measured inside a control loop, and the damping or servo that keeps the instrument usable suppresses the response to be measured. The naive FRF taken against the injected reference then returns the suppressed closed-loop response rather than the plant. The P&S reference-based estimate — the ratio of period-averaged spectra against the drive monitor, which is the true plant input — cancels the controller and returns the open-loop plant, with no controller model. ::: {#d3b00222 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="A high-Q mode under a velocity damper: recover the open-loop plant through the live loop"} cl = md.closed_loop_campaign(seed=0) md.closed_loop_fig(cl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The loop suppresses the resonance by the factor in the title, and the naive estimate returns that suppressed curve. The reference-based estimate, on the same data, lands on the open-loop plant to a fraction of a percent — the controller is cancelled rather than fitted. A plant inside a loop is therefore not a reason to reach for special-case tooling: the same multisine pipeline handles it. (The DARM page, [example 08](../examples/08-darm-calibration.qmd), is the same idea on the gravitational-wave readout; the suspension closed loop here is the general statement.) ## 7 · The consolidated comparison One table, four excitations, the five figures of merit, populated from the campaigns above on the representative suspension plants of this page. ::: {#7368e581 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Everything, side by side (real numbers from the campaigns)"} display(md.headtohead_table(head, v_leak, c_sweep, cl)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Head-to-head on the representative suspension plants of this page. RMS for the optimal arm is at the budget that MATCHES flat's σ (F=14); RMS is plant-referred (the binding limit is DAC saturation after the whitening chain, not modeled here, so no peak/crest column is shown). The closed-loop reference FRF recovered the open-loop plant to 1.4% through a 48× suppressing loop.** | excitation | time to target σ | RMS drive (plant-referred) | leakage bias (high-Q peak) | per-bin noise model? | closed-loop safe? | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | swept sine | ~122× a multisine window | 1.00 | none (1 line) | per-line coherence | yes, but slow | | broadband random | never (biased) | 1.00 | -16% (leaks) | no (assumed) | no (S_yx/S_xx biased) | | flat multisine | > budget passes | 1.00 | -1% (leakage-free) | yes (period scatter) | yes (reference-based) | | optimal multisine | 2 passes | 0.27 | -1% (leakage-free) | yes (period scatter) | yes (reference-based) | ::: ::: The pattern: the swept sine is safe and exact but slow; broadband random is fast but biased on the high-Q peaks and unsuited to use as the quantitative estimator in a loop; the flat multisine addresses leakage and the loop but spends its budget indiscriminately; the optimal multisine retains every multisine property and additionally converts the Fisher structure of the plant into either less time or less drive. ## 8 · How any subsystem uses the package The pipeline is plant-agnostic. Identifying a new subsystem requires two things — a channel backend (how to inject and read) and a prior model — and then the loop: ```python from system_ident.backends.base import ChannelBackend # implement inject()/read()/ramp_down() from system_ident.backends.twin import TwinBackend # or the provided twin/CDS/DARM backends from system_ident.model import TFModel from system_ident.loop import SysIDLoop from system_ident.design.pintelon import PintelonSchoukensDesigner from system_ident.estimators.gml import GMLEstimator from system_ident.safety import Watchdog, SafetyLimits # 1. a prior — even a rough one; the first pass is prior-robust over f0·(1±u) prior = {"POS": TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 50.0)], gain=300.0)} # 2. a backend that speaks the relevant channels (twin shown; swap in a CDS/hardware backend) backend = TwinBackend(plant, {"EXC": "POS"}, {"RSP": "POS"}, drive_channels={"DRV": "POS"}) # DRV = the loop's drive monitor # 3. the loop wires designer + estimator + watchdog and runs: # measure noise → design optimal multisine → inject (default phase=Schroeder, a # free choice that does not affect the FRF; Tukey-ramped for a safe start) # → leakage-free reference FRF → ML fit → CRB → redesign → repeat loop = SysIDLoop(backend, GMLEstimator(), PintelonSchoukensDesigner(), Watchdog(SafetyLimits.from_config(config))) result = loop.run(config, prior, seed=0) # result.models["POS"] is the fit ``` Everything on this page is that loop with a different `config` and `prior`. The worked [examples 01–08](../examples/index.qmd) walk the same path from a single resonance through a coupled 2×2 suspension, the compiled CDS twin, and the DARM readout — each running the identical diagnostic set (excitation design → time series → magnitude/phase/coherence Bode → residuals → Cramér–Rao recovery → drive safety → convergence). ## 9 · Assumptions, failure modes, and when each alternative applies No method is without cost. The optimal multisine carries assumptions and failure modes, and the alternatives are better in specific regimes. **What the optimal multisine requires.** - **Synchronous, integer-period capture.** The leakage-free guarantee holds only if the drive is periodic over the analysis window and the acquisition is sample-synchronous. Losing period alignment (clock drift, dropped samples, a non-integer window) decays the leakage advantage toward the windowed-random case. On CDS this is a wiring requirement, not a given. - **A prior.** The optimal design is only as good as the model it is computed from. The package mitigates this with a prior-robust first pass (power spread over `f0·(1±u)`), but a badly wrong prior, an over-specified model order, or a missing mode can misallocate the budget. The mode of operation is iterative: a broad pass, then concentrate. - **A stationary, linear plant over the window.** The whole-band-in-one-window property assumes the plant does not drift mid-measurement and responds linearly to the drive. Strong nonlinearity or fast non-stationarity breaks the model the CRB is computed against. - **In a comb-sensitive band, a comb is a cost.** A multisine puts many lines in band at once. Where those lines contaminate a science band (e.g. DARM during observation), that footprint is a real operational price the swept sine's single line largely avoids — run in non-observing time, or use known phases so the lines subtract. - **The binding actuator limit is at the DAC, and this simulation is plant-referred.** In LIGO the hard saturation limit is at the DAC (counts/volts), with whitening and actuation filters between the digital excitation request and the DAC. Crest factor is not invariant under filtering, so a waveform optimised for low crest in plant/force units (Schroeder phasing, concentrated power) is reshaped by the whitening chain and can present an unrelated — generally higher — peak at the DAC. This demonstration models only the plant-referred frame and omits that chain, so it makes no crest-factor or peak-drive claim; the in-band-power (RMS) numbers it reports are plant-referred. A peak/crest optimisation is a DAC-frame, filter-aware problem — push the design through the whitening/actuation model and minimise the peak there. That is future work, and these plant-referred numbers cannot stand in for it. **When to pick an alternative instead.** - **Swept sine** — a single line to high SNR, a quick spot check, or any case where transparency and full power on one frequency matter more than band coverage. - **Broadband random** — a fast qualitative whole-band picture, coherence diagnostics, or disturbance/floor characterisation where a percent-level peak bias is irrelevant. - **Flat multisine** — when no usable prior exists and leakage-free, self-error-barred whole-band coverage is wanted before the concentration points are known. (It is the package's own first pass.) The optimal multisine is the appropriate default when all of the following hold: time is scarce, drive is bounded, the plant is high-Q, the loop is closed, and at least a rough prior exists — which covers most LIGO subsystems most of the time. The package implements one pipeline, and the position taken here is that the situation determines which knob, and which excitation, applies. ## References Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*, 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — periodic / leakage-free measurement; multisine design and Schroeder phases (§4); dispersion-function optimal input design (§5.4.2); the reference-based (closed-loop) FRF; and the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimator with its Cramér–Rao efficiency. [LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information expressions for suspension parameters (the form carried by `fisher.fisher_matrix`). [LIGO-G1400084](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G1400084) (Larry Price) — original motivation and prior work. See also `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md` for the DARM-specific comparison and its literature trail.
